text: I keep coming back to the moment at the station this afternoon. Dev's train was late by forty minutes and I had nearly given up and gone to the car, and then there he was at the end of the platform with that ridiculous green rucksack he's had since university, waving with both arms like a child. Two years. Two years of calls that cut out and birthdays over a screen, and suddenly he was just there, solid, smelling of train and coffee, apologising for the delay as if he could have done anything about it. We walked to the car and neither of us said anything important, we talked about the weather and whether the chip shop near Mum's was still open, and I didn't mind at all. I have been grinning at the kettle for the last hour. The house feels different with his shoes by the door.

Long day, good day. The market was heaving by nine and I'd sold out of the sourdough by half ten, which has never happened before, and then a woman I didn't recognise came up and said she'd driven twenty minutes because her neighbour wouldn't stop going on about my rye. Twenty minutes! For bread I made in a kitchen with a broken extractor fan. Afterwards Tomasz helped me pack the van and we ate the two squashed cinnamon buns nobody had wanted, sitting on the tailgate with our feet dangling, and he said this was starting to look like an actual business and I laughed and said don't jinx it. My back is sore and my hands smell of flour and I can't stop smiling. I'll sleep well tonight. Up at four again tomorrow and for once I'm not dreading it.

We took the kids to the lake today because the forecast said rain and I decided I didn't care. It did rain, for about twenty minutes, and we sheltered under the big oak and Mina counted the drips off the leaves and Arjun tried to catch them in his mouth and got one in the eye. Then the sun came out and the whole surface of the water went silver and the children ran straight in with their clothes on, screaming, and I stood at the edge with the towels thinking: this is it, this is the thing I'll remember when they're grown and don't want to come. We had soggy sandwiches in the car with the heater on full. Arjun fell asleep with his mouth open before we reached the motorway. I feel light. I feel like we got away with something.

Found the box of Dad's letters while clearing the loft for the insulation people. I'd forgotten they existed, or I'd made myself forget. His handwriting is exactly as I remember it, that slanted capital D he was so proud of, and the first one I opened was to Mum from the year before I was born, telling her about a job interview and a landlady who didn't like his shoes. He was twenty-six. He sounded so hopeful and so young. I sat on the loft ladder for an hour reading them while the men waited in the van and then I had to tell them to come back tomorrow because I couldn't trust my voice. It's been nine years in March. People say it gets easier and it does, mostly, but today it was like a door I'd painted shut just came off its hinges. I miss him so much it's physical. I've put the box by my bed. I don't know if I'll open it again this week.

The adoption agency called at lunchtime. It was the woman with the kind voice, the one who always asks how I'm doing before she says anything else, so I knew before she got to it. The birth mother has decided to parent. Which is her right, and I mean that, I would never want a child taken from someone who wants them. I said all the correct things. I said we understand, and please tell her we wish her well, and yes we'd like to stay on the list. Then I went into the stairwell at work and sat on the bottom step for a long time. The room is painted. Ruth did the yellow stripe herself and it took her three evenings. We'd stopped saying the name out loud but we both knew what it was. I don't know how to go home and look at that door. I don't know how to tell her. I'm writing this in the car park because I can't make myself start the engine.

Kept busy all day so I wouldn't have to think about it, and then I made the mistake of sitting down. The flat is so quiet without Biscuit. Fourteen years. I keep hearing his claws on the kitchen floor and turning round. His bowl is still by the radiator because I can't decide whether washing it and putting it away would be worse than leaving it. The vet was gentle and it was quick and he wasn't frightened, I held his head and told him he was good, and he was, he was the best. Sunil texted to ask if I wanted company and I said no, and now I think I was wrong, but it's late. I know he was a dog. I know people lose far more. I just didn't realise how much of the shape of my days was him: the walk at seven, the sigh when I got the lead out, the weight against my feet while I read. Tomorrow at seven there will be nothing to do.

Results come through tomorrow between nine and eleven, the letter said, by text or by phone depending on what they find, and I have read that sentence so many times I've started to see meaning in it that isn't there. Depending on what they find. I've already done the thing where I plan both versions of tomorrow: the version where I text Hana a thumbs-up from the bus and the version where I have to call her from somewhere private. I cleaned the bathroom at eleven at night. I've organised the spice drawer. I know statistically it's almost certainly nothing, the doctor said as much, she said these things are very common and we check to be safe, and I believed her at the time, but it's two in the morning now and statistics don't live in my chest the way this does. My heart keeps doing a little skip when the phone lights up for anything. I'm going to try to sleep. I'm not going to sleep.

First day in the new job tomorrow and I've laid my clothes out like a schoolchild. Three different routes planned in case the trains are off. I've looked up everyone on the team and I know what two of them studied and where the manager used to work, which I now worry is weird and I should pretend I don't know. The thing is, I was good at my old job. I knew where everything was and who to ask and which jokes landed. Tomorrow I'll be the person who doesn't know how the printer works, and I'll have to ask someone, and they'll be kind about it, and I'll feel about nine years old. Omar keeps saying everyone feels like this and they only hired me because they thought I could do it. I'm sure he's right. I'm also sure I will lie awake until at least one going over what to say when they ask me to introduce myself. My stomach has been in a knot since about four this afternoon.

Jamie's school emailed to say there'd been an incident at break and they'd like to speak to us in the morning. That's all. An incident. I've phoned twice and got the answering machine, and I have now spent four hours constructing every possible meaning of that word. Did he hurt someone, did someone hurt him, is it the thing with the older boys again that he swore was sorted. He came home perfectly normal, ate his tea, argued about screen time, and when I asked how school was he said fine in the voice that means fine. I don't want to interrogate him. I also don't want to walk into that office tomorrow and be blindsided. Priya says I'm catastrophising and that if it were serious they'd have called, not emailed, and that's true, that's a very sensible point, and I have written it down and read it back and it has done nothing whatsoever for the feeling in my chest.

Rain all day so I stayed in and didn't fight it. Made a pot of soup around noon that I'll be eating until Thursday, read sixty pages of the book Nadia lent me, fell asleep on the sofa under the blanket with the cat on my shins. Woke at four with that grey light coming in and the radiator ticking and for a while I just lay there listening to the gutter and didn't reach for my phone, which I think is the first time in months. There's nothing I'm waiting for. Nothing urgent in the inbox, nobody I owe a call. I've noticed my shoulders are somewhere lower than they usually are. I used to think days like this were wasted, and I'd feel I had to earn the evening by having done something. Today I don't feel that at all. The soup was good. The book is good. The rain is still going and I'm going to run a bath.

Sat with Grandad for most of the afternoon. He doesn't say much now and some days he isn't sure who I am, but today he knew, or he was happy to pretend, and we watched the birds on the feeder outside his window for an hour without either of us needing to fill the silence. A robin, two blue tits, a fat pigeon he laughed at. The nurse brought tea and he held the cup in both hands the way he always did. I used to find these visits unbearable, I'd drive home shaking, trying to fix something that couldn't be fixed. Somewhere in the last few months that's gone. I'm not fighting what's happening to him any more. I just sit, and he sits, and the birds come and go, and when I kissed his head to leave he patted my hand twice, which is what he did when I was small. Drove home slowly with the radio off.

Finished the last session with the counsellor today, the one we'd agreed would be the last back in September. I thought I'd feel wobbly about it and I don't, particularly. I walked out into the car park and it was just an ordinary Tuesday, cars and a bin lorry and someone's dog barking, and I stood there and noticed I wasn't scanning for the next thing to go wrong. That's the change, I think. Not that nothing goes wrong, plenty still does, Tariq's job is still uncertain and the boiler still makes that noise. It's that I don't live braced against it all the time. She asked me at the end what I'd say to the person who walked in a year ago and I said: you're allowed to put the bags down. I'd like to remember that. I bought a coffee and drank it slowly on the bench outside the library before I drove home, for no reason except that I could.

The neighbours did the whole thing without telling me. When I got back from the hospital with Mum's prescriptions and three bags of shopping and about four percent battery left in my own body, the front lawn had been mown, the recycling had been put out, and there was a casserole on the step with a note from Mrs Okafor that said 'no need to return the dish, eat when you can'. I stood on the path and cried like an idiot. I've lived here six years and I've barely spoken to half of them beyond hello. I didn't ask for any of it. I don't think I'd have known how. Tonight Mum ate properly for the first time since Friday because somebody else's cooking tastes like food again, and I ate too, and I have been thinking about how much I owe people I don't really know. Tomorrow I'm going to write them all a card. I don't know how to say it properly but I'll try.

I want to write down what Kemi did this term before I forget the details and it just becomes 'she was helpful'. She noticed in week two that I was going quiet in seminars and instead of asking me about it in front of everyone she sent a two-line message that said she'd got the readings in a shared folder if that was easier and no need to reply. Then she made sure to sit next to me and ask my opinion on things quietly before the discussion started so I'd have something ready. She never made it a thing. She never once said 'are you okay' in that voice. By week eight I was talking in class without planning it first. I don't think she knows she did any of this. When I tried to say thank you at the end of today's session she looked genuinely confused and said she'd just wanted someone to split the readings with. I'm going to miss her over the summer more than I expected to.

The physio signed me off today, nine months after the crash. I walked out of the building without the stick, and there was a moment at the bottom of the steps where I reached for the handrail out of habit and then didn't need it, and I stood there like an idiot with my hand in the air. Nine months. There was a week in January when they weren't sure I'd get full movement back in the knee and I lay in that bed doing the maths on what my life would be if I couldn't climb again. I never wrote that down at the time because writing it felt like agreeing to it. I want to thank the woman who stopped on the hard shoulder and held my hand until the ambulance came. I never got her name. I want to thank Lena for driving me to every single appointment and never once sighing about it. I want to thank the nurse on the night ward who told me, when I asked at three in the morning, that she'd seen worse knees walk out dancing. I'm going to the climbing wall on Saturday. Just to look. Maybe to touch the holds.

Third time this month the system has gone down at four in the afternoon, which is exactly when every parent in the building is trying to finish and get out the door, and third time the response from IT has been a ticket number and a smiley face. I have now re-entered the same forty records twice. Twice! Because the autosave they promised in March doesn't actually save and nobody will admit that. I raised it in the team meeting and Gareth said he'd 'take it away', which is what he says about everything, and I watched it go into the notebook where things go to die. I am not asking for miracles. I am asking for the tool I'm required to use to stay switched on during the hours I'm required to use it. I left at six-fifteen with the records still not done and the childminder charged me for the extra half hour, which is money I'm essentially paying because a server is held together with string. I'm too wound up to sleep and I have to do it all again tomorrow.

Spent the whole day on chapter four and ended with fewer words than I started with. I know that's sometimes how it goes, I've read all the advice about trusting the process and sitting with the problem, but it's been eleven days on this chapter now and I'm starting to resent the characters. Every version of the scene has the same hole in the middle. I tried writing it from Mireille's point of view, I tried cutting it entirely and jumping to the hospital, I tried a letter, and every time I get to the same spot where she has to decide and I don't know what she'd do, which is ridiculous because I invented her. Bea asked at dinner how it was going and I bit her head off for no reason and then had to apologise, which took longer than it should have. Deadline is the twelfth. I'm nowhere near. I'm going to go and stare at the ceiling and hope the ceiling has ideas.

Forty-five minutes on hold to the council, then cut off. Rang back, forty minutes, got through to someone who said it wasn't her department and transferred me, and the transfer rang out. I've now spent the best part of my only free morning this week trying to get a parking permit for the carer who comes to see Nan, a permit that the council's own letter said I'd need, and I am no closer than I was at nine o'clock. The website says apply online and the online form says apply by phone. I've written down every reference number and every name and I have a page of them and they add up to nothing. Nan kept asking who I was shouting at and I wasn't shouting, I wasn't, but I could hear my own voice and it wasn't good. The carer's parking fine arrives next week presumably. I'll pay it myself rather than put her through this. I'm so tired of every simple thing being a fight.

Tickets booked. Actually booked, with a confirmation number and everything, so I can't back out this time. Four weeks from Thursday I'll be landing in Lisbon on my own with a rucksack and a very bad grasp of Portuguese and no plan beyond the first two nights. I've been talking about doing this since I was twenty-two and I'm thirty-four and I kept finding reasons: money, work, then Fraser, then after Fraser the sheer effort of imagining myself as someone who does things. I pressed the button at lunch and my hands were actually shaking and then I had to go back into a meeting about procurement and pretend I was a normal person who hadn't just done something enormous. I've already downloaded three maps. I've already started a list of words. I keep opening the confirmation email just to look at it. Can't sit still. Can't stop smiling at the wall.

They said yes. The gallery said yes! I read the email three times standing in the queue at the post office because I didn't believe the first two, and then I made a noise that made the man in front turn round. Eight paintings, the back room, the whole of November. I've been sending work out for six years and I have a folder of polite nos thick enough to stop a door. I called Ayesha from the pavement and she screamed so loud I had to hold the phone away, and then she said she'd always known, which is a lie, she's spent six years telling me gently to keep the day job, but I love her for saying it. I've already started planning which ones. The big blue one, obviously. The two of the estuary. I need to frame things. I need to find out what a private view actually involves. I have no idea how I'm going to get any work done this week. I keep standing in the studio just looking at the walls.

Twelve days until Bapu and Ba land. Twelve! Their first time out of India, first time on a plane that long, first time seeing the flat, first time meeting Isla's family properly instead of on a cracked video call where Ba keeps holding the phone to her ear. I've cleaned the spare room twice. I've bought the pressure cooker Ba asked for in a tone that suggested she didn't trust ours. I've made a list of places: the coast, the castle, the market on Sunday where the man sells the sweetcorn Isla says is 'the closest to home you'll get'. I keep catching myself grinning on the bus. Isla's parents have offered to do a lunch and I have been coaching her dad on how to say the names, and he has been practising, which makes me want to cry a bit. There's a version of this where it all goes wrong and everyone is awkward and the weather is dreadful. I don't care. They're coming. I'm counting sleeps like a child.

My brother said something at the weekend that I haven't been able to put down. We were washing up after Mum's birthday and he said, not unkindly, that I've been 'managing' everyone in the family since I was about twelve, and that he sometimes wonders what I'd be like if I stopped. I laughed it off at the time. But I've been turning it over for three days now. He's right that I do it. I make the plans, I smooth the arguments, I remember the appointments. I'd always thought of that as just who I am, the helpful one, and I'm starting to wonder how much of it was a role I took on because nobody else did and then forgot I could put down. I don't think it's made me unhappy, exactly. I think it's made me tired in a way I'd stopped noticing. I don't know what the alternative looks like. I'd like to find out, slowly, without anyone getting hurt in the experiment.

Twenty years today since I moved to this country with two suitcases and a phone number on a piece of paper. I didn't mark it, no one else knows the date, but I walked past the bus stop where I waited that first morning, not knowing the buses didn't take coins, and I stood there a while. The girl who got off that plane couldn't have imagined this: the house, the accent my children tease me for, the way I dream in a language my mother doesn't speak. I've lost things too. I can't remember the words for some kitchen tools. My cousin Farida's children call me the aunt from abroad. There are jokes at home I no longer get. Some days this feels like a trade I made without reading the terms. Most days it just feels like a life, mine, odd-shaped and real. I bought a coffee from the kiosk by the bus stop. The man asked if I was waiting for someone. I said no, just remembering.

Cleared out the old studio today because the lease is up, and I found the sketchbooks from the first year of the business, when it was just me and Leon and a borrowed printer. Pages of logos that never happened, a plan for a shop we were going to open in the arcade that's now a vape place. We were so sure. We argued about kerning for whole afternoons as if the world depended on it. I don't miss being that broke but I do miss being that certain. Somewhere between then and now the work got bigger and the arguments got smaller and more polite, and I'm not sure that's entirely a good thing. Leon's in Berlin now doing something with an agency and we message about twice a year. I kept two of the sketchbooks and put the rest in the recycling, and then I took one back out again. I'm not sure what I think. I'm not sure I need to decide tonight.

Day thirty without a drink. I'm writing the number down because the counsellor said to notice it and because a month ago I genuinely did not think I'd get here. It hasn't been pretty. There was the dinner at Jo's where I held a glass of sparkling water so hard I thought it might break, and the Friday after the review when I walked past the off-licence three times. But I'm here. I slept properly last night for the first time in I don't know how long, actually slept, no four a.m. heart racing. My skin looks different. Saira said I seem more there, which is a strange compliment and I'll take it. I'm not going to pretend I've got it beaten. I know what the leaflets say about month two. But something in me has shifted from 'I have to do this' to 'I might actually be able to do this', and that's not nothing. Day thirty-one tomorrow. I'd like to see what day sixty looks like.

The consultant used the word 'manageable' today and I have been carrying it around like a warm stone. Not cured, she was careful about that, and there's a long road of appointments and adjustments and learning what my body can and can't do now. But manageable. After five months of nobody being able to tell me why I was falling asleep in meetings and losing words mid-sentence, there's a name for it and a plan and a sheet of paper with next steps on it. Jonah cried in the car park, which he never does, and then pretended it was hay fever in November. I didn't cry. I felt something uncoil in my chest that's been wound tight since the summer. I know there'll be bad days. I know the medication might take a few tries. But tonight for the first time since this started I can imagine a version of next year where I'm doing my job and walking the dog and not frightened all the time. That feels like a lot.

Had the first proper conversation with Ella in nearly a year. She called, not me, which matters, and we talked for forty minutes about nothing much, her flatmate's cat, a film she'd seen, the fact that the café on the corner has finally changed its coffee. We didn't go near the thing. I didn't bring it up and neither did she and I think that was right for a first go. But she laughed at something I said, properly laughed, and at the end she said 'speak soon' and sounded like she meant it. I've spent a year being told by everyone, including myself, to give her space, and I did, and it was the hardest thing I have done as a parent. I'm not kidding myself that one phone call fixes it. There's a lot still unsaid and some of it will be hard to hear. But the door's not locked. She called me. I'm going to hold on to that for a while.

Night three of Rosa's chest infection and I've lost track of what day it is. She's okay, the doctor said it's viral and just needs riding out, but she can't lie flat without coughing herself awake so I've been sitting up with her propped on my chest in the armchair, and I'm getting maybe ninety minutes of sleep in twenty-minute pieces. Marco's doing the days, bless him, but he starts at six and someone has to be functioning. I made a cup of tea this afternoon and found it cold three hours later, untouched, on top of the microwave. I put the milk in the cupboard. I called the dog by Rosa's name. My eyes feel like they've been rolled in sand. She's asleep on me now, finally, properly, and I should be sleeping too but I'm too wired and too flat at the same time, if that's a thing. I'm not upset. I'm just empty. I would give a great deal for eight hours in a dark room.

Double shift again because Dan's off sick and there's nobody else trained on the till and the kitchen at the same time. Eleven hours on my feet, the last three of them with that dull band of pain across my lower back that I've stopped mentioning to anyone because there's nothing to be done. Got home at eleven, ate cereal standing up at the counter, sat on the edge of the bed to take my shoes off and just stayed there for a while looking at the carpet. The flat needs hoovering. There's a letter from the bank I haven't opened. My phone has four messages I don't have the words for. I don't feel sad exactly, I'm too worn down for sad. I just want to lie down in a way that goes on for longer than a night. Alarm's set for six-thirty. I'll be fine. I'm always fine. I'd just like, for once, to find out what it feels like not to be running on the last bar.

Finally finished the tax return at half past eleven and I feel like I've been through a wringer. Four years of receipts in a shoebox because I kept telling myself I'd set up a proper system in January, every January, and never did. Six hours today with the laptop on the kitchen table and the cat sitting on the one bank statement I needed. Nour brought me a sandwich at some point and I don't remember eating it but the plate's empty. It's done. It's submitted. I don't even feel relieved yet, I just feel hollowed out, like my brain has been scraped. My eyes are gritty from the screen and I've had that tension headache behind the right eye since about four. Going to have a bath and then sleep for as long as my body lets me. Tomorrow I'm going to buy a folder and some of those plastic sleeves. I know I've said that before.

I found out from a group chat. A group chat. Eight people knew that Kieran had moved the launch date and that my team would be doing the weekend, and not one of them, not one, thought to tell the person who actually runs that team. I had to read it on my phone in the lift and then walk into the office and act like I already knew. When I asked him about it he did the little laugh, the one he does, and said it must have slipped through the cracks and he was sure I'd be flexible. I have been flexible for three years. I have covered his meetings and fixed his slides and told clients he was 'in transit' when he was asleep. I'm not angry that we're working the weekend. I'm angry that I don't exist in that man's head as a person who needs to be told things. I went for a walk at lunch so I wouldn't say anything I'd have to apologise for later, and I'm still shaking a bit now. I will be saying something tomorrow. I'll do it calmly. But I will be saying it.

The landlord came round unannounced again, let himself in while I was in the shower, and when I came out in a towel he was standing in my kitchen 'checking the boiler'. He's been told. He has been told in writing, twice, that he must give twenty-four hours' notice, and both times he's nodded and said of course, and both times he's turned up whenever he likes because he knows I'm on a rolling contract and he knows what the market's like and he knows I won't make a fuss. Well. I'm making a fuss. I wrote to the agency tonight, formally, with dates. I've started a log. My hands were shaking when I typed it and not from fear. Mel says I should just move and she's probably right but I'm sick of the answer to every bad landlord being that the tenant should uproot her whole life. It's my home. He doesn't get to walk through it like a corridor.

Mum rang to say Auntie Beth had 'passed on some thoughts' about my parenting at the christening. Apparently I'm too soft with Theo, apparently a boy his age shouldn't still be having bedtime stories, apparently she worries. She didn't say any of this to me. She said it to Mum, in front of Mum's friends, knowing it would get back. That's how she's always done it. I've spent thirty years watching her do it to my cousins, to Mum, to anyone who doesn't push back, and I've always let it go because she's old and she's family and it isn't worth the row. Tonight, listening to Mum relay it in that apologetic voice, I felt something go hard in me. He's six. He had a bad year. I will read him stories until he's forty if he wants them. I am not going to ring her and shout, I'm not giving her that. But the next time she starts in front of me I am going to look her in the eye and say no, calmly, once, and let it sit there. I'm done pretending I didn't hear.

Nothing happened today and I want to write it down anyway. Woke before the alarm, no reason, just awake, and lay there listening to Adaeze breathe for a while. Made coffee. Watered the tomatoes, which are finally doing something after weeks of sulking. Worked from the kitchen table with the back door open and the smell of next door's jasmine coming through. Nobody needed anything urgent. In the afternoon I fixed the squeaky hinge on the bathroom door that's been squeaking since we moved in, two years, and it took four minutes, and I stood there opening and closing it like a fool. We ate outside. We talked about maybe getting a second-hand bike for her. We did the crossword and got stuck on the same clue we always get stuck on. I'm not happy in the fireworks sense. I'm just here, in a life that fits, and I noticed it, and I wanted to say so.

Three months in the new flat and I think I've stopped thinking of it as the new flat. I know which stair creaks. I know the bus timetable without looking. The man at the corner shop knows I want the Sunday paper and puts one aside. After the divorce I thought I'd feel like a visitor in my own life for years and instead there's this: a small place with my books on shelves I put up myself, slightly crooked, and a window with a plant on it that's still alive. Hamid came for dinner on Saturday and said it felt like me, which is the nicest thing anyone's said in a while. I made the lamb thing. We stayed up too late. I don't want more than this at the moment. I'm not saying forever. I'm saying that for the first time since everything, enough feels like enough, and I'd forgotten that was a feeling you could have.

End of the allotment year. Dug over the last bed this afternoon while the light went orange, and sat on the upturned bucket afterwards with a flask of tea and my boots caked, looking at the rows. Not a brilliant year: the courgettes went mad, the carrots were a joke, the slugs had every single lettuce. But the beans were the best I've grown and the shed roof held, and old Bernard from two plots down gave me a bag of his apples and told me my soil was 'coming on', which from him is practically a medal. I've got the winter garlic in. There's nothing else to do until February except turn the compost and think. I like this bit. The year's work is done, badly in places and well in others, and it's all in the ground now and there's a kind of settledness in that. Home for a bath and a very large plate of the beans.

Everyone in the office has somewhere to be on a Friday. By half five it had emptied out, phones going, 'have a good one', and I was still there pretending to finish a report because the alternative was going back to the flat. It's been eight months since I moved here for this job and I've managed precisely one friendship, with Noor from the third floor, and she's on maternity leave now. I've joined things. The running club, the pottery evening, the book group where everyone already knew each other from a previous book group. People are perfectly nice. Nobody's unkind. I just go home afterwards and the quiet closes over me like water. I rang Mum on the walk back and she asked if I was eating properly and I said yes, and we talked about her neighbour's roof, and when I hung up outside the building it was worse than before I'd called. I've put the telly on for the sound of voices. I know this is a phase. I'd like the phase to end.

The house is so big now the children have gone. Eli went in September and I thought I'd adjust by Christmas, and now it's nearly spring and I'm still setting the table for three and then quietly putting one place back. Raj works late and when he's home he's tired and we sit in different rooms with different screens and it's not that anything's wrong, it's that nothing's happening. I used to complain that I never had five minutes to myself. Now I have whole evenings and I walk around the house touching things. I called Eli yesterday and he was lovely and busy and had friends waiting and said he'd ring at the weekend, and I said of course, and I meant it, I want him to have all of that. I just hadn't understood that being needed was the thing holding my days together. I don't know who I am in this house without someone to make a packed lunch for.

Went to Dani's wedding on my own because the invitation said plus one and I didn't have one. It was beautiful, she looked radiant, I cried at the vows like everyone else. And then the meal, and the table of couples, and the dancing, and the slow song where everyone paired off and I went to the loo and stayed there for the whole of it reading the back of a hand soap bottle. Nobody did anything wrong. People were warm. Dani's mum squeezed my hand and said my turn next and meant it kindly. But I drove home at eleven down the motorway in the dark with the radio off and the feeling I've been keeping at arm's length for two years sat down in the passenger seat and put its feet up. I'm thirty-eight. I have good friends and a job I like and a flat I chose. And tonight there was nobody to tell about the speeches, or the cake, or the fact that the DJ played the song from our first holiday, and I had to hold that on my own.

I passed. I actually passed. Three attempts, two instructors, one minor meltdown in a Tesco car park in February, and today I drove round that test route with the examiner writing nothing down for forty minutes and at the end he said 'that's a pass' and I asked him to say it again. I'm forty-one. Every single person in my family drives. My little sister passed at seventeen and has been gently offering lifts ever since in a tone I've chosen to find loving. I told myself for twenty years that I was a 'public transport person' and the truth is I was terrified and ashamed of being terrified. Not any more. I drove Hollie to football practice tonight, just me and her, with the L plates off, and she said 'Mum you're actually doing it' in a voice of such amazement that I nearly cried at the roundabout. I did it. I did the hard thing. I keep looking at the certificate on the fridge.

Presented to the board this morning. Forty minutes, no notes, all eleven of them including the chair who has a reputation for cutting people off at slide three. He didn't cut me off. He asked two questions, both of which I'd prepared for, and at the end he said 'that's the clearest case I've heard for this in two years'. I walked back to my desk and sat down and realised my legs were shaking, which they hadn't been in the room, as if my body had agreed to wait until it was over. Six months ago I couldn't speak in a team meeting of eight without my voice going. I did the course, I practised in the mirror like a lunatic, I recorded myself and made Jun listen to the recordings, which he did with great patience. And today I stood up in front of the people who decide things and I was good. Not fine. Good. I'm going to let myself have this one.

Yusuf's first week at school is done and I want to write this down for me, not for him. On Monday he clung to my leg at the gate and I had to peel him off and walk away with him screaming and I sat in the car and shook. On Tuesday he cried but let go. On Wednesday he held my hand to the door and said 'you can go now Baba' in a voice that was about eighty percent brave. Today he ran in without looking back. I know this is normal. I know every parent in that playground has a version of this story. But I'm the one who got him there: the stories about school for six months, the practice walks, the lunchbox he chose himself, the five mornings of standing at that gate and not crying where he could see. His teacher caught me at pick-up and said he'd helped another boy who was upset. He's four. I did all right with this one. I'm allowed to think that.

The list has stopped being a list and become a wall. Grandma's care assessment is Tuesday and I still haven't found her birth certificate. The car failed its MOT on three things and the garage wants it back Thursday, which is the day the boys have the dentist and I have the appraisal. Ife's school has sent four emails about a trip I apparently needed to pay for by yesterday. The bathroom ceiling is doing that thing again. Work's launched a 'wellbeing week' with daily lunchtime sessions I am expected to attend while also delivering the thing that's due Friday. I sat down tonight to work out what to do first and I couldn't. I actually couldn't. I looked at the page and all the items were the same size and the same urgency and I just sat there with the pen in my hand. Dele asked if I was okay and I said I'm fine, I'm just thinking, and he went to bed, and I'm still here with the pen.

Three weeks into the new role and I'm underwater. Everyone assumes I know things I don't know because the person before me knew them, and there's no handover document, there's just a shared drive with four hundred folders named things like 'FINAL v3 USE THIS'. I've got nine projects on the go and I can't tell you with confidence what stage any of them are at. Today I was in back-to-back calls from nine until half three with no lunch, and in every call someone asked me a question I had to say I'd come back to them on, and I have a list of things I've said I'll come back to people on that's now two pages long. Camille says it's always like this for the first month. Maybe. But I came home tonight and stood in the hallway with my coat on for ten minutes because taking it off felt like one more thing. I don't know where to start. There is no start. It's all middle.

Everybody wants a piece of the wedding and I'm the only one holding the plate. Mum wants the church. Pete's mum wants the hotel where she had hers. Pete wants 'whatever makes you happy', which is a lovely thing to say and completely useless. The venue needs numbers by Monday and nobody will tell me whether they're bringing partners. My sister has opinions about the dress I haven't bought. The florist has stopped replying. I have a spreadsheet with eleven tabs and tonight I opened it and shut it again because I couldn't face the colours. This is supposed to be a happy thing. I know it's a happy thing. But I sat on the stairs tonight with the phone ringing in the kitchen, probably Mum, probably about the church, and I just let it ring, and I put my head on my knees and breathed for a while, because every single decision has four people attached to it and every single one of them loves me and I cannot breathe.

Notes from today so I don't forget. Boiler service done, engineer says the pressure valve will want replacing within the year, quoted roughly two hundred for parts and labour, written on the yellow sheet by the fuse box. Changed the car insurance to the cheaper quote, new policy starts on the first, documents are in the email folder under 'house'. Prescription collected for Mum, twenty-eight days this time instead of fourteen so that's one less trip. Spoke to Alan next door about the fence: he's happy to split the cost, he'll get a quote from his brother-in-law, he thinks mid-November. The leak under the sink is the washer not the pipe, bought the washer, will do it at the weekend. Still need to: renew the parking permit, chase the dentist about the recall letter, measure the back window for the blind, return Sanjay's drill. Bins are Thursday this week because of the bank holiday.

Travel day. Train from the central station at 07:42, changed at the junction with eleven minutes to spare, second train on time. Read the quarterly report on the way, made notes in the margins for the three o'clock. Arrived 11:20, walked to the hotel, room not ready so left the bag and went to the client office. Meeting ran 14:00 to 16:30: agreed the revised timeline, they'll send the amended scope by the end of next week, we owe them the cost breakdown by the fifteenth. Kwame joined by video for the second half. Dinner at the place by the river Hiro recommended, the fish was good, bill was within the daily limit. Back at the hotel by nine. Return train tomorrow at 15:10, so there's time for the second meeting at ten and a sandwich. Expenses so far: two train tickets, one taxi, dinner. Receipts in the front pocket of the laptop bag.

Meal plan and shopping for the week, writing it here because the fridge whiteboard has died. Monday: the chicken thing with the rice, leftover for Tuesday lunch. Tuesday: pasta, Wren's cooking. Wednesday: out, it's Lou's birthday, booked the Thai place for seven-thirty for six people. Thursday: soup from the freezer, bread from the market if I pass it. Friday: pizza, the boys are choosing toppings. Saturday: Dad's coming so a roast, he likes the lamb, check if the butcher has a shoulder. Sunday: whatever's left. Need from the shop: rice, onions, two tins of tomatoes, coconut milk, the oat milk Wren likes, bin bags, dishwasher tablets, a card for Lou. Already have: pasta, chicken in the freezer, potatoes. Budget for the week is the usual, slightly over if the lamb's dear. Check the meter reading before Friday because the email said they'd estimate otherwise.
